name: Femi Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher at the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't take money from AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Can you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the health and education reporter for the website of a regional evening paper, so hospitals, GP surgeries, schools and the university. I'm in by half seven, check the hospital trust's board papers and the school inspection reports that came out overnight, and file a couple of short stories before nine. Then I try to get out: a school gate, a ward that's closing, a parent who's emailed in. I use an AI tool now and then, mostly to summarise a hundred-page board report, but I always read the bits that matter myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best bit is when a parent rings back to say a story got their son's school transport sorted. I like being useful, the way my dad is useful in his pharmacy. What wears me out is the website wanting six stories a day when two good ones would serve readers better. I rent a one-bed flat across the river, I've got about five months of money saved, and I'm hoping to propose to my girlfriend Priya next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. A world where nothing much happens. That's a fairly normal Tuesday for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI turned out to be a handy summariser and not much more. I'd say it at the Friday five-a-side and probably leave it there, because I don't post opinions online. My editor would want a piece on what the hospital trust spent on AI pilots, and I'd happily write that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI wasn't what kept me up anyway. The group froze hiring last year, two people on the news desk left and weren't replaced, and the six-stories target keeps going up. None of that goes away because AI is hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, stay on the health beat, and try to break one proper story a month to make myself harder to cut. I'd keep saving, maybe push from two hundred to three hundred a month, because a ring and a wedding aren't cheap. I'd also go back to my old journalism tutor about some shifts teaching a module at the college, just to see if I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. Steady but with one eye on the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned teaching. Where does that idea come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum was a primary teacher for thirty years, and she's always said I'd be good at it. I used to roll my eyes. But a classroom is a real place with real children, and it has a certain safety to it, which I didn't value at twenty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the team would you worry about, even in this quiet world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carol, who runs our live blog and the traffic and weather updates. That's exactly the routine stuff a summariser can do, so her hours might get trimmed even here. Carol (the live blog editor) has two teenagers and a husband who's been off work with his back.

say: AI turned out to be a **handy summariser** and not much more.
He'd happily write about what the trust spent on **AI pilots**.
think: AI was never his main worry; the **hiring freeze** is.
The **six-stories target** keeps rising whatever happens with AI.
do: Break **one proper story** a month to be harder to cut.
Raise savings from two hundred to **three hundred** a month for a ring and wedding.
Ask his old tutor about teaching **college shifts** to test the idea.
feel: **Uneasy**: steady, but with one eye on the door.
S0.quote: The group froze hiring last year, two people on the news desk left and weren't replaced, and the six-stories target keeps going up.
fieldNote: His unease comes from a **hiring freeze** that predates any AI talk.
Teaching is a seed planted by his **mum**, now looking more sensible to him.
He measures himself by **usefulness**, like his father the pharmacist.
He spots that **Carol's** routine live-blog work is exposed even in a quiet world.

steps.text: Break one exclusive health or schools story every month
Raise monthly savings to three hundred for the ring and wedding
Teach a few college journalism shifts to try out teaching

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Writing, checking, answering customers. That's a lot of my week, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say newsrooms should use it for the boring bits, the board papers and the inspection summaries, and put reporters back on the street. I'd say that in the newsroom without sounding like I'm against it, because I'm not. I'd also say people need proper apprenticeships to move into new work, not just a payment and a pat on the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the website would use it to hit the six stories with fewer people. The quick stories I file before nine, an AI could file those by itself. That leaves the out-and-about part, which is the part I'm good at but also the part that's slow and expensive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good at the tools other reporters are already using, starting in January, so I'm the one checking machine copy rather than being replaced by it. I'd keep the savings going and put off the engagement party, though not the proposal. I'd sign up for a part-time teaching qualification taster at the university, a short evening course, by next September.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like a quiet tightening in the chest when the editor calls a meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put off the party but not the proposal. Why that line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the proposal is about Priya and me, and the party is about money. My dad would say you don't let a bad year decide who you marry. The party can wait for a good year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if your job shrank in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, partly the readers, who won't pay for local news, and partly the group's bosses, who keep chasing clicks. I wouldn't blame the technology itself. A tool is a tool; what matters is who decides how it's used.

say: Newsrooms should use AI for the **boring bits** and put reporters on the street.
People need proper **apprenticeships** to move into new work, not just payments.
think: The website would hit **six stories** with fewer people.
His **quick morning stories** are exactly what AI could file alone.
do: Learn the **tools** colleagues use from January, to check machine copy.
Keep saving and **postpone the engagement party**, but not the proposal.
Take an evening **teaching taster** course at the university by September.
feel: **Anxious**, a quiet tightening whenever the editor calls a meeting.
S1.quote: My dad would say you don't let a bad year decide who you marry.
fieldNote: He separates **love** from **money**: proposal yes, party later.
He blames **readers and bosses**, not the technology itself.
He picks up tools only **once others** have proven them, true to type.
Teaching moves from idea to a **concrete course**.

steps.text: Learn the AI checking tools colleagues use, starting in January
Keep saving three hundred a month
Propose to Priya but postpone the engagement party
Take an evening teaching taster course by next September

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's not time to do anything properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after each other, families and communities first, and not wait for the government to fix it. I'd say that at the temple and at the five-a-side. At work, I'd say we should still be the ones holding hospitals and schools to account, even if a machine writes the copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is finished by about 2029. Almost all of it is reading, writing and asking questions, and that's exactly what arrives first. The robots coming three years later don't change anything for me, because there's no hands-on part of my job a robot would be needed for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply straight away for a teacher training place starting next September, and look at the paid on-the-job route so I'm not living off savings. I'd cut back hard: give up the car, cancel the gym, and tell Priya we're doing a small wedding. If the training didn't work out, I'd ask my dad about doing the counter and deliveries at the pharmacy for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Honestly, I'd lie awake doing the sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI comes first here and robots later. Does teaching look safe to you against that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer, not safe. AI could mark essays and plan lessons the day it arrives, so the thinking side of teaching changes in 2028 too. But somebody has to stand in a room with thirty fourteen-year-olds and keep them in their seats, and I don't see a robot doing that well even in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Priya, the night you decided?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That my job is going, that I've got a plan, and that I still want to marry her this year if she'll have a man who's starting again. Priya (my girlfriend) is an occupational therapist, so her work is hands-on and probably lasts longer than mine. I'd feel strange about her carrying us, but I'd get over it.

say: Look after **families and communities** first, not wait for government.
Reporters should still hold **hospitals and schools** to account.
think: The robots coming later **change nothing**, since his job has no hands-on part.
do: Apply now for a **paid teacher training** place starting next September.
Give up the **car** and gym, and plan a small wedding.
Ask his dad about **pharmacy work** if training falls through.
S2.quote: Somebody has to stand in a room with thirty fourteen-year-olds and keep them in their seats, and I don't see a robot doing that well even in 2031.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** within the two years and plans a career switch.
He sees that teaching's **thinking side** changes on the AGI date too.
Priya's **hands-on** therapy work becomes the household's steadier income.
He prefers **family and community** help over the state, in line with his views.

steps.text: Apply for a paid teacher training place starting next September
Give up the car and cancel the gym membership
Plan a small wedding with Priya this year
Ask his dad for counter and delivery work at the pharmacy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's a bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as before, but I'd be more upbeat. I'd say five years is long enough to retrain properly if people start now. I'd probably write a series about local teachers, nurses and pharmacists and how they see it, because that's my beat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the job still goes, just around 2031 or 2032. Five years means I can finish a teacher training year and get two or three years in a classroom before the big change. That's a real head start compared with people who wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reporting for another year and do evening study to get my maths back up, because maths teachers are always wanted. Then I'd start teacher training in autumn 2028. Priya and I would marry in 2027, a normal wedding, and keep renting until I'm qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can manage. Five years feels like a plan instead of a scramble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why maths rather than English, given you write for a living?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because everyone with a degree like mine wants to teach English. Schools are crying out for maths teachers, and my dad would say pick the job that's needed, not the one you fancy. I got a good grade at school and I've done enough hospital budgets to be comfortable with numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss about reporting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being let into places. Sitting with a nurse on a night shift because she wanted someone to see it. Teachers don't get that; they're in one building. I'd miss the variety more than the bylines.

say: Five years is long enough to **retrain properly** if people start now.
He'd write a series on how **teachers, nurses and pharmacists** see it.
think: The job still goes, just around **2031 or 2032**.
Five years gives him a **head start** in a classroom before the change.
do: Report one more year while studying **maths** in the evenings.
Marry Priya in **2027** and keep renting until qualified.
feel: Anxious but **manageable**, more a plan than a scramble.
S3.quote: Schools are crying out for maths teachers, and my dad would say pick the job that's needed, not the one you fancy.
fieldNote: He picks **maths** for need, not for love, echoing his father.
Extra time turns a scramble into a **sequence**: study, train, teach.
The wedding returns to **normal size** with five years of warning.
He'd miss **being let in** to places more than his byline.

steps.text: Study maths in the evenings for a year to prepare for teaching
Keep reporting health and schools until training starts
Marry Priya in 2027 and keep renting until qualified

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Now that's a different conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for anyone willing to work at it. I'd say firms and colleges should offer proper apprenticeships for people changing careers, and that families should help each other through. I wouldn't say much online; I'd write about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think I can have a good run in journalism first, maybe make it to health editor, and still switch by my mid-thirties. Thirty-seven is not too late to start teaching. My mum's friend started at forty and became a deputy head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the beat for the next four or five years and aim for health editor. I'd start a teaching qualification around 2031, while the thinking AI is still arriving, so I'm in a classroom before it lands. Priya and I would buy a small house in a couple of years and think about children around 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. Uneasy, I suppose, because the end is still coming, but I can live with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy a house. How does that square with your job ending in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy something small that Priya's salary could cover on its own if it had to. That's my rule. Her work as an occupational therapist is hands-on and has a few more years than mine in any version of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change the plan and leave journalism sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the group started cutting the health beat or merging us with the morning paper. Then I wouldn't wait for health editor. I'd go to teacher training straight away.

say: Ten years is enough for **anyone willing** to work at it.
Firms and colleges should offer **apprenticeships** for career changers.
think: He can aim for **health editor** before switching in his mid-thirties.
Starting teaching at **thirty-seven** is not too late.
do: Stay on the beat four or five years and aim for **health editor**.
Buy a **small house** Priya's salary could cover alone.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with some unease because the end still comes.
S4.quote: I'd buy something small that Priya's salary could cover on its own if it had to.
fieldNote: The decade gives him a **career in two halves**: reporter, then teacher.
His house rule is **cautious**: Priya's wage alone must cover it.
A **merger** of papers is the trigger that would speed him up.
He's uneasy rather than anxious, since teaching looks **secure** for him in this timeline.

steps.text: Stay on the health and schools beat and aim for health editor
Buy a small house that Priya's salary alone could cover

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my whole job is thinking work and two years is barely a training course. What would help is paid teacher training routes that open quickly, so people like me can earn while we retrain, and newspaper owners giving staff honest notice instead of a Friday meeting.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the hospitals and schools themselves. If nobody local is reading the board papers, a ward can close and the town finds out from a sign on the door. I'd want someone to still be checking, even if it isn't me.

headlineQuote: If nobody local is reading the board papers, a ward can close and the town finds out from a sign on the door.
portrait: Femi is a **27-year-old** health and education reporter for a regional evening paper's website.
He uses AI **now and then** to summarise board reports, and always reads the key parts himself.
He rents alone, has about **five months** saved, and plans to propose to Priya, an occupational therapist.
His standing worry is a **hiring freeze** and rising story targets, before AI enters it.
Across the AGI pictures he plans to become a **maths teacher**, faster as the warning shrinks.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his job is all thinking work and two years is too short.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid teacher training** routes that open quickly.
Owners giving staff **honest notice** of cuts.
